---
title: "Scattered data"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using ConvolutionInterpolations, Plots, Printf, Random
default(size = (720, 400), linewidth = 2, framestyle = :box, fontfamily = "sans-serif")
rms(v) = sqrt(sum(abs2, v) / length(v))                   # root mean square, used throughout
```

Measurements rarely come on a grid. The Julia package handles scattered points by fitting a
grid to them: a convolution interpolant on a grid over the points' bounding box, whose knot
values are chosen so that the interpolant matches the points. The result is an ordinary gridded
interpolant, so everything on the other pages — evaluation anywhere, derivatives, integrals —
works on it unchanged. `fit_scattered` does the fit and returns the grid;
`convolution_interpolation(points, values)` does the fit and returns the interpolant.

The Python port does not include scattered data yet; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd)
tracks the port.

## Two modes

- `mode = :smooth`, the default, smooths: it minimises the misfit at the points plus a
  roughness penalty whose weight is chosen by generalized cross-validation, and reports the
  noise level it found. For measured data, which carry noise.
- `mode = :exact` interpolates: the fit passes through every point to machine precision, and
  among the grids that do, the smoothest is chosen. For trusted, noise-free data only — noise
  would be reproduced exactly and amplified between the points.

The default differs from the gridded constructors, which always interpolate, because
scattered data are usually measurements.

## Noisy measurements

Points in the unit square, one per column of the matrix, with a smooth signal and noise:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(1)                                           # reproducible points and noise
pts = rand(2, 800)                                        # 800 scattered points in 2D, one per column
signal(x, y) = sin(3x) * cos(2y)                          # the signal
σ = 0.05                                                  # the noise standard deviation
vals = [signal(p[1], p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts)]         # the signal at the points
noisy = vals .+ σ .* randn(800)                           # measured with noise

knots, grid, info = fit_scattered(pts, noisy)             # the fitted grid, smoothing chosen by cross-validation
itp = convolution_interpolation(knots, grid; kernel = :a4, bc = :poly)   # the interpolant, with the kernel the fit used
info                                                      # the smoothing parameter and the estimated noise
````

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
x1, x2 = extrema(pts[1, :])                               # the fit's domain is the points' bounding box
y1, y2 = extrema(pts[2, :])
xf = range(x1, x2, length = 150)                          # a fine grid over it, for measuring the error
yf = range(y1, y2, length = 150)
itp_fine = [itp(xi, yi) for xi in xf, yi in yf]           # the interpolant on it
exact2 = [signal(xi, yi) for xi in xf, yi in yf]          # the signal on it
println("| | the noisy points | the fitted interpolant |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| rms error against the signal | %.4f | %.4f |\n", rms(noisy .- vals), rms(itp_fine .- exact2))
println()
println("| | generated | estimated by the fit |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|")
@printf("| noise standard deviation | %.4f | %.4f |\n", σ, info.noise)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
p1 = heatmap(xf, yf, itp_fine', title = "interpolant", clims = (-1, 1), colorbar = false, aspect_ratio = 1)
scatter!(p1, pts[1, :], pts[2, :], markersize = 1.5, markercolor = :white, markerstrokewidth = 0.5, label = "")
p2 = heatmap(xf, yf, exact2', title = "signal", clims = (-1, 1), colorbar = false, aspect_ratio = 1)
plot(p1, p2, layout = (1, 2), size = (760, 380))
```

The grid is sized from the point density, as fine as the points resolve, and the smoothing is
set by the penalty weight, not by the knot count; the [smoothing page](smoothing.qmd) compares
this fit with Gaussian smoothing on gridded data.

## Trusted data

With `mode = :exact` the interpolant passes through the points. Since it is a gridded
interpolant underneath, its derivatives and integrals come from the same object; the wrapper
forwards `derivative`, so a box integral over the points' domain is four evaluations of the
twofold antiderivative:

```{julia}
Random.seed!(2)
pts2 = rand(2, 300)                                       # 300 trusted points
vals2 = [signal(p[1], p[2]) for p in eachcol(pts2)]       # the signal, without noise

itp_x = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact)                      # interpolates the points
dx_x  = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact, derivative = (1, 0)) # ∂/∂x of the same fit
ii_x  = convolution_interpolation(pts2, vals2; mode = :exact, derivative = (-1, -1)) # ∫∫ from the corner

box = (0.2, 0.7, 0.3, 0.8)                                # x₁, x₂, y₁, y₂ of a box inside the domain
boxint(F, x1, x2, y1, y2) = F(x2, y2) - F(x1, y2) - F(x2, y1) + F(x1, y1)   # inclusion–exclusion
itp_x(0.4, 0.6), dx_x(0.4, 0.6), boxint(ii_x, box...)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
exact_box = (cos(3 * 0.2) - cos(3 * 0.7)) / 3 * (sin(2 * 0.8) - sin(2 * 0.3)) / 2   # ∫∫ sin(3x)cos(2y) over the box
println("| | f(0.4, 0.6) | ∂f/∂x (0.4, 0.6) | ∫∫ over the box |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| from the fit | %.8f | %.8f | %.8f |\n", itp_x(0.4, 0.6), dx_x(0.4, 0.6), boxint(ii_x, box...))
@printf("| exact | %.8f | %.8f | %.8f |\n", signal(0.4, 0.6), 3cos(3 * 0.4) * cos(2 * 0.6), exact_box)
```

```{julia}
#| output: asis
viol = maximum(abs(itp_x(p[1], p[2]) - v) for (p, v) in zip(eachcol(pts2), vals2))   # the fit at the points
@printf("The largest deviation of the interpolant from the data at the points is %.1e.\n", viol)
```

## Clustered points and adaptive grids

An exact fit needs the grid to separate the points: two points in one grid cell cannot both be
matched. A uniform grid sized from the mean density cannot do that for clustered points, and
the fit says so with a warning and returns the least-squares fit instead. `grid = :adaptive`
places the knots of each axis at the quantiles of the points' coordinates, so a dense band of
points gets a dense band of knots — and where the points are dense because the function
varies fast there, as in a measurement campaign that samples a layer closely, the dense knots
are also where the accuracy is needed:

```{julia}
layer(x) = tanh(40x)                                      # a steep layer at the centre
u = range(-1, 1, length = 60)
xs = sign.(u) .* abs.(u) .^ 2                             # 60 points, clustered towards the layer
pts1 = reshape(xs, 1, :)                                  # as a 1 × n matrix
ys = layer.(xs)                                           # trusted values

ku, vu, viol_u = fit_scattered(pts1, ys; mode = :exact)                    # uniform grid: warns
ka, va, viol_a = fit_scattered(pts1, ys; mode = :exact, grid = :adaptive)  # adaptive grid
itp_u = convolution_interpolation(ku, vu; kernel = :b5, bc = :poly)        # the kernel the fit used
itp_a = convolution_interpolation(ka, va; kernel = :b5);                   # a nonuniform grid: the nonuniform :b5 kernel
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
xr = range(-1, 1, length = 1001)
itp_d = convolution_interpolation(collect(xs), ys; kernel = :b5)   # for comparison: the nonuniform kernel with its knots at the points
println("| | uniform grid | adaptive grid | knots at the points |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
@printf("| knots | %d | %d | %d |\n", length(ku[1]), length(ka[1]), length(xs))
@printf("| largest deviation at the points | %.1e | %.1e | %.1e |\n", viol_u, viol_a, maximum(abs.(itp_d.(xs) .- ys)))
@printf("| largest error against the function | %.1e | %.1e | %.1e |\n", maximum(abs.(itp_u.(xr) .- layer.(xr))), maximum(abs.(itp_a.(xr) .- layer.(xr))), maximum(abs.(itp_d.(xr) .- layer.(xr))))
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
plot(xlabel = "x", legend = :topleft)
scatter!(xs, ys, markercolor = :white, markerstrokewidth = 1.5, label = "points")
plot!(xr, itp_u.(xr), label = "uniform grid")
plot!(xr, itp_a.(xr), label = "adaptive grid")
plot!(xr, layer.(xr), color = :black, linestyle = :dash, label = "function")
scatter!(ka[1], fill(-1.1, length(ka[1])), markershape = :vline, markersize = 6, label = "adaptive knots")
```

Exactness at the points and accuracy between them are different things. On the same clustered
points sampled from a function that is smooth everywhere, the uniform fit's least-squares
compromise is as accurate as the adaptive fit's exact match, often more so, because the
uniform grid spends its knots evenly where the function needs them evenly. The adaptive grid
pays off when the points are dense where the function is steep, or when the values themselves
must be reproduced. The last column of the table is the nonuniform kernel with its knots at
the points — the plain interpolant through the same samples. The fit is more accurate than
that as well: among the grids that match the points it takes the smoothest, and the knots it
has between the points serve that end.

An adaptive grid is nonuniform, so the interpolant on it is the nonuniform one of the
[nonuniform page](nonuniform.qmd): derivatives are available, antiderivatives are not. The
spacing ratio of adjacent knots is capped by the `ratio` keyword, which keeps the nonuniform
kernels well conditioned; raise it for strongly graded data. The grid is still a tensor
product, so it helps when the point density is roughly separable along the axes — a boundary
layer, a log-scaled axis — and not for isolated clusters.

## Knots and points

Two keywords size the grid. `oversample` is the number of knots per mean point spacing, with
mode-dependent defaults (lower for `:smooth`, where the penalty does the regularising; higher
for `:exact` in two or more dimensions, where random points share cells more often);
`gridsize` fixes the knot count outright. Both modes warn when the grid is the limit: `:exact`
when the points could not all be matched, `:smooth` when the fitted smoothing would need a
finer grid than the budget allows. The [scattered-data benchmark](../benchmarks/scattered.qmd)
has the convergence of both modes with the point count, and timings.
